transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-12
Time: 14:30 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jenna Lee (AtlasML Head of ML), Marco Ruiz (AtlasML Infra Lead), Priyanka Nair (AtlasML Research)

Summary:
This was a deep technical review focused on quantization tradeoffs (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ), accuracy regressions we've seen in early pilots, and runtime impacts on latency/throughput, KV cache behavior, and batching. AtlasML is evaluating Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) for sensitive clinical-genomics assistant use cases and wants a pilot to validate model quality after quantization as well as latency SLOs. They asked for benchmark artifacts and a plan for a 1-week pilot.

Topics covered:
- INT8 vs FP8: perf vs accuracy tradeoffs
- GPTQ and AWQ: tooling, calibration, and known regressions
- Runtime effects: KV/prefix cache, continuous batching, cache hit patterns
- VPC/on-prem deployment considerations: KMS, SOC2, audit logs, network egress
- Next steps and pilot plan, artifacts to share

Action items called out in call (verbatim):
- Priya to run microbenchmarks
- Marco to send prompt distributions and sample dataset
- Samir to share AWQ/GPTQ tuning notes and spreadsheet

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Samir from Redwood here, Priya is on the call too. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Jenna: Good, thanks. Excited to dig through the quantization stuff \u2014 have a few concerns around accuracy drop for clinical prompts.
[00:00:20] Priya: Great, we can run through our benchmarks. Quick agenda: walk through INT8/FP8, then GPTQ/AWQ experience, and runtime considerations \u2014 caching, batching, then deployment notes. Sound good?
[00:00:30] Marco: Yep. We're mostly interested in 1) whether INT8 is safe for our models, 2) what AWQ buys us vs GPTQ, 3) what the latency impact is, specifically P99 for short prompts.
[00:00:45] Priyanka: Also want to understand quantization-induced hallucinations \u2014 we've seen small but concerning errors when we tried off-the-shelf GPTQ.

[00:01:10] Priya: Cool. So first, INT8 \u2014 it's the fastest path usually because it maps nicely to our optimized kernels, gives biggest throughput gains on GPU + inference stack. But it is lossy and you'll see accuracy regressions, especially on out-of-distribution or calibration-sensitive tokens, e.g., small named entities in clinical text.
[00:01:35] Samir: Right. In our internal tests INT8 often reduces latency by ~1.6x-2x vs FP16 baseline but can give measurable drop in certain eval sets. FP8 is a newer option \u2014 pros are smaller quantization error compared to naive INT8 in some layers because of dynamic exponent range, but hardware support and ecosystem is still spotty. We've run FP8 prototypes on Hopper/Grace-class hardware with mixed results.
[00:02:05] Jenna: When you say "mixed" \u2014 is that because runtimes are immature or because the models need re-calibration?
[00:02:10] Priya: Both. FP8 requires careful scaling and we've seen some frameworks treat it differently. Also kernel availability matters; if your infra doesn't have FP8 kernels we fall back to emulation which kills perf.

[00:02:40] Marco: Ok. GPTQ vs AWQ \u2014 we've read the papers. GPTQ is stable-ish, but AWQ claims better accuracy at lower bitwidths. What's your experience?
[00:02:51] Priya: Good question. GPTQ is a well-understood post-training quant approach and tends to be robust if you do layerwise calibration and per-head handling. AWQ (we've seen it as "AQW" in some transcriptions before haha) has shown impressive numbers at 3/4-bit but it's newer; it often requires careful per-layer tuning and sometimes bespoke quantization tables. In practice AWQ often wins on downstream accuracy for smaller bitwidths, but it's more brittle if you change sequence lengths or prompt distribution.
[00:03:22] Priyanka: That brittleness is what worried us \u2014 in our internal run we saw a 2-3% drop on entity extraction after GPTQ, and one-off hallucinations were more frequent.
[00:03:31] Samir: That's consistent with other customers. Important point: accuracy regressions are dataset- and prompt-distribution dependent. We recommend running a targeted eval set (your clinical prompts) during the quantization step. We'll help instrument that.

[00:03:55] Priya: On runtime side, KV cache behavior matters a lot. With quantized kernels you can see differences in memory footprint and cache alignment. Continuous batching and our prefix caching layer can mask some of the latency, but worst-case P99 for single-token streaming can be sensitive to quantization because of decoding jitters and kernel dispatch overhead.
[00:04:20] Marco: Can you elaborate on "cache alignment"?
[00:04:23] Priya: Sure. If the quantized tensor layout changes (e.g., 8-bit packing vs 4-bit packing in AWQ), the way we store KV in RAM and on GPU differs, and that affects how often we hit prefetch-friendly access patterns. That can affect latency for short-law sequences. For long sequences, the benefits of smaller caches often improve throughput because you avoid swapping.
[00:04:52] Jenna: So for our use case \u2014 short clinical prompts (avg 32 tokens) and then a 150-token generated report \u2014 what's the recommended path?
[00:05:00] Samir: For that pattern we usually start with GPTQ at 8-->4 or 8-->bits depending on the model; often a hybrid approach: keep critical layers at higher precision and quantize the rest. If you need the absolute lowest latency and can tolerate a small accuracy delta, INT8 is attractive, but we should test on your eval set. For maximum accuracy retention at low bits AWQ could be tried, but it needs more tuning.
[00:05:30] Marco: What about FP8? Any reason to consider it?
[00:05:33] Priya: FP8 can be great for some transformer architectures because it preserves dynamic range, which helps with very deep models or unstable training dynamics. But for inference-only stacks it's still early: limited kernel support, potential emulation overhead, so it's usually not the first choice. If you have Hopper/Grace plus the right libs, it can be worth a POC.
[00:06:00] Priyanka: On the topic of routing and model variants \u2014 can Redwood runtime do automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant if a request hits a quality guardrail?
[00:06:09] Samir: Yes \u2014 our smart routing supports policy-based fallback. You can define thresholds and for requests where e.g., a classifier flags low confidence, we can re-issue to an FP16 or a dedicated higher-precision model. That does increase cost and latency for that request but keeps quality.
[00:06:35] Marco: For VPC/on-prem deployment \u2014 we need details on KMS integration and audit log retention. How mature is Redwood Private here?
[00:06:43] Samir: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM) and we wire in audit logs to your SIEM via syslog/S3 sinks. There's also RBAC and SSO/SAML integration. We can share the security whitepaper after the call.
[00:07:05] Jenna: Any known network egress overheads if we run in a VPC with Private control plane?
[00:07:11] Priya: For VPC with private control plane we minimize egress. Control plane calls are minimal; most of the inference traffic stays within your VPC if you deploy the Private runtime. There are initial handshake calls to our control plane for management unless you're fully air-gapped. We'll document exact endpoints and data flows.
[00:07:35] Samir: Back on benchmarks \u2014 we recommend three runs: 1) per-request latency (P50/P95/P99) on representative prompt set, 2) throughput with steady-state batching to get tokens/sec, and 3) quality/regression checks on your eval set (ROUGE/EM/F1 or custom metrics). We'll provide benchmark harness and a spreadsheet.
[00:07:58] Priyanka: For the quality checks, do you support A/B testing in the runtime to collect real traffic signals?
[00:08:04] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary/A/B rollouts and collects token-level metrics and diffed output snapshots for eval sets. For private, that same tooling works through our control plane or via local telemetry sinks depending on deployment mode.
[00:08:30] Marco: A bit implementation-focused \u2014 what's the expected GPU memory reduction for AWQ vs INT8 vs GPTQ?
[00:08:38] Priya: Rough ballpark: INT8 can reduce model memory by ~2x vs FP16 in our stacks; GPTQ (4-bit variants) can be ~2.5-3x depending on packing; AWQ at 3-bit can be 3-3.5x but remember AWQ has per-layer metadata that adds small overhead. FP8 doesn't always give as much reduction vs FP16, but it can allow smaller accumulators and better per-kernel performance in ideal hardware. These are rough numbers \u2014 we'll put precise figures in the spreadsheet after the microbenchmarks.
[00:09:10] Jenna: About hallucinations \u2014 is the common mitigation to do layerwise higher-precision for critical layers? Any heuristics?
[00:09:18] Priya: Yes, a common heuristic: keep the attention and final MLP layers at higher precision, quantize middle MLP blocks more aggressively. Also doing a small calibration dataset drawn from your worst-case prompts helps. In some cases we do mixed-precision where embeddings are FP16, mid layers are INT8/GPTQ, and output head is FP16.
[00:09:45] Samir: Another mitigation is to instrument regression tests \u2014 Redwood's eval pipelines can automatically run your prompt set on both baseline and quantized variants and flag diffs beyond thresholds. We'll help set that up for the pilot.
[00:10:02] Priyanka: On runtime latency \u2014 how much does batching help for our short prompt + long generation pattern?
[00:10:09] Priya: Batching helps system throughput but can hurt single-request latency. We use adaptive batching: small queues for low-latency requests and larger pools for high-throughput background jobs. For your pattern it's possible to configure an accelerator pool that favors low-latency streaming while another pool handles higher-throughput report generation. That keeps P99s reasonable.
[00:10:35] Marco: For the pilot, we'd want reproducible results. What artifacts do you need from us to kick off the 1-week run?
[00:10:42] Samir: We'll need: 1) representative prompt set (Marco to send), 2) sample dataset for accuracy/regressions, 3) target SLOs (P99 latency target, CPU/GPU constraints), 4) whether you prefer AWQ/GPTQ or both tested. We'll run INT8, GPTQ (4-bit), and AWQ (if you want) and share the spreadsheet.
[00:11:05] Jenna: We will send prompts and a 500-sample eval set. Also need to validate SOC2 artifacts before pilot.
[00:11:12] Samir: We'll send SOC2 docs and the security whitepaper. Also include network diagram and KMS options.
[00:11:25] Priya: Quick note: if you're running on-prem with non-NVIDIA GPUs we've had customers with AMD/Graphcore where kernel availability is the blocking constraint. We recommend identifying exact hardware SKU early.
[00:11:40] Marco: We're standardizing on A100/NVIDIA for now, so should be fine.
[00:11:48] Priyanka: Any caveats on tokenization differences after quantization? We've seen small token-splitting changes in one run and that messed with downstream metrics.
[00:11:57] Priya: Tokenization should be independent of quantization; if you saw differences that suggests upstream tokenizer model mismatch or subtle float-to-int rounding leading to rare decoding differences. We'll include tokenizer parity checks as part of the baseline vs quant check.
[00:12:20] Samir: Let's run a quick example \u2014 Priya, show a microbenchmark result (screen share reference noted).
[00:12:25] Priya: (describes) On a 7B model baseline FP16 we see 120 tokens/sec. INT8 optimized path ~210 tokens/sec with P50 latency down by ~40%. GPTQ 4-bit gives ~260 tokens/sec but we saw a 1.8% drop on an entity extraction eval. AWQ 3-bit gave 290 tokens/sec on the same hardware but needed per-layer recalibration to avoid a 3% drop on the same metric.
[00:13:02] Jenna: Those are helpful numbers. Can you share the raw spreadsheet?
[00:13:05] Samir: Yes, Samir will share.
[00:13:10] Marco: About instrumentation \u2014 how do we capture cases where quality guardrails trigger fallback in production?
[00:13:16] Priya: Our tracing includes request-level metadata and we can emit a flag when fallback happens plus the original and fallback outputs. Redwood Console can aggregate those events and produce a report. For private installs the telemetry can be sent to your SIEM.
[00:13:35] Jenna: Any legal/procurement blockers you foresee for a pilot?
[00:13:40] Samir: Typical asks: DPA, standard security questionnaire, and specific KMS/HSM terms. We can start with our standard pilot contract and attach SOC2 docs.
[00:13:55] Priya: One more runtime nuance: KV cache eviction policies interact with quantized model memory. If you pick an aggressive 3-bit AWQ you free more GPU memory and can keep larger KV cache, which helps long-context throughput. But for short context patterns the smaller per-token compute may dominate end-to-end latency.
[00:14:20] Marco: Good to know.
[00:14:22] Samir: Ok, to recap action items and next steps \u2014 Marco will send prompt distribution and sample eval by 2026-09-16. Priya will run INT8/FP8/GPTQ microbenchmarks on a representative sample and post results by 2026-09-19. Samir will share AWQ/GPTQ tuning notes, the benchmark spreadsheet, and security whitepaper by 2026-09-14. We'll schedule the 1-week pilot to start 2026-09-20 pending docs.
[00:14:45] Jenna: Sounds good. Anything else?
[00:14:48] Marco: Not from me. Thanks all.
[00:14:51] Samir: Thanks everyone \u2014 we'll follow up with links and the spreadsheet.
[00:14:57] End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., AWQ typed as AQW), and some proper nouns mangled. Transcript stops at end.
